author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: The Apprenticeship of Asking
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fourth expansion pass
content:
The boatbuilder was sixteen, furious, and holding a plank upside down.

Lio's sketch was pinned beside the slipway. It was covered in revisions, including a note in thick chalk: *Sela's crate must not slide*. That was the part I looked at while Maui looked at the shape of the prow.

“Very elegant,” he said.

Lio did not look impressed. “It's a working boat. It needs to stay upright when the water moves.”

“I know something about water.”

“Then you know it won't care how famous you are.”

Maui went silent. Mini Maui on his arm put its tiny hands over its face, which was not helping.

Fen came down the steps with the original order. “Lio is responsible for the design review. Maui, you are here as an assistant unless the apprentice asks you to demonstrate.”

“I have sailed across oceans!”

“And you're very welcome to discuss that after the safety checks.”

Lio was only sixteen. I could see how much courage it cost them to say no to somebody who filled half the doorway and half the valley's stories. They did it anyway.

“Please hold the plank level while I mark the second support,” Lio said.

Maui reached for the wood, then stopped with his hand open.

“Like this?”

“Lower. No—there. Keep it there.”

He obeyed. It was a small thing, a demigod being told where to put his hands, and it held more value than another tale about him saving somebody who hadn't needed saving.

I put the measurements into the workshop ledger. There would be time to ask him about the ocean later. Today the boat belonged to its builder and the person who had commissioned it.

I knew the plank was upside down because Fen had marked the side facing the water in bright blue chalk. The apprentice knew it too. They had been staring at the mark for nearly a minute, as though determination might turn the wood.

Maui reached for the plank.

"Here! I know boats. Hand me that and I'll make it look easy," he said, reaching for the plank before Lio had even answered. His grin was all confidence, which would have been more persuasive if the apprentice hadn't looked ready to bite him.

Lio pulled it away.

"I can do it."

"I know. But it'll be faster if—"

"I said I can do it."

I was carrying a bucket of clean water and trying very hard not to interfere.

A moment later I interfered.

"Turn it clockwise," I said.

Lio turned toward me.

"I know."

I closed my mouth.

Fen watched the three of us with the expression of someone considering whether the dock needed apprentices, heroes, or a large sign prohibiting both.

"Start again," Fen said.

Lio put the plank on the sawhorses.

Maui stepped back. So did I.

The new boat was a shallow coastal skiff intended for short journeys between the Tideglass landing and the sheltered inlet. It wasn't a legendary vessel. It wouldn't make anyone famous. It would carry crates of tea, rope, and occasionally the people who had jobs too small for a great voyage but too important to miss.

Lio had been apprenticed to Fen for six weeks. They knew how to measure the ribs, cut a clean mortise, and keep sharp tools out of other people's reach. They also knew, in the way teenagers sometimes know things very loudly, that they had to prove everything without assistance.

Maui had volunteered to teach the knotwork. He had not been asked to build the boat.

He was having trouble understanding the distinction.

By midday Lio had finished fitting one rib and rejected four pieces of advice. Maui had demonstrated the same knot eight times. I had corrected two measurements that hadn't needed correcting.

Maui knelt beside the practice frame and demonstrated the knot again. His hands moved with astonishing speed. The rope became a neat loop before Lio had managed to locate the working end.

"See? Beautiful. Effortless. You may applaud."

Lio folded their arms.

"Or," Fen said from behind us, "you could teach a person instead of auditioning for your own statue."

Mini Maui appeared on his forearm and pointed at Lio's empty hands.

"You're all against me," Maui said.

"Only your teaching method," Fen replied.

He stared at the rope, thinking. Then he untied the knot and tossed the line back to Lio.

"All right, apprentice. Here's the trick: you tell me what you think the rope wants to do, and I'll tell you how badly you're lying to it."

"Ropes don't want things," Lio said.

"Then why do they spend their lives trying to escape us?"

Lio laughed. They tried again, slowly. Maui kept his own hands to himself and narrated the mistakes with such extravagant descriptions that by the end of the hour the apprentice was calling every tangled loop a *demigod disaster*. Maui pretended to be offended, but he finally looked like a teacher who was having fun watching someone else learn.

Fen called a break.

"Both of you," they said, pointing to Maui and me, "come with me."

We followed them to the workshop.

They shut the door.

"Maui, what are you teaching Lio?"

"How to tie the rib lashings."

"No. You're showing them how quickly Maui can tie rib lashings."

He winced.

Fen looked at me.

"And you?"

"I'm helping with measurements."

"You're taking the pencil every time the numbers look uncertain. What does Lio learn from that?"

I stared at my hands.

"Not much."

Fen nodded.

"This is an apprenticeship. They need to make mistakes within safe limits. We stop them before a mistake harms someone. We don't stop them because the work is taking longer than we like."

Maui crossed his arms.

"What if the boat sinks?"

"Then we don't launch it until it passes inspection."

That seemed obvious once someone said it.

I thought about the last several months. Maui and I had spent so much time talking about respecting other people's choices that I'd become proud of how well I could explain it.

Explaining wasn't the same as practicing.

"What should we do?" I asked.

Fen handed me a blank inspection sheet.

"Ask Lio what help they want. Then give it."

Maui looked at the paper.

"That's all?"

"That's a surprising amount of work for people who enjoy talking."

We returned to the slipway.

Lio was sanding the rib we'd left on the sawhorses. Their jaw was set. They didn't look up when we approached.

Maui stopped at a respectful distance.

"I think I've been showing off," he said.

Lio glanced up.

"You think?"

"I know."

They looked startled.

He held out the rope.

"Would you like me to demonstrate once and then let you try? Or would you rather work it out?"

Lio considered the question.

"Demonstrate once. Slowly."

Maui smiled.

"Slowly. I can do that."

I tried not to laugh.

He took nearly a full minute to tie the knot. It was the least dramatic demonstration I'd ever seen from him. He named each loop, explained which part carried the load, and showed how the line could be loosened for inspection.

Then he handed the rope over.

Lio got it wrong.

He waited.

They tried again.

This time it held.

"Good," Maui said.

Lio grinned before they could stop themself.

I looked down at my inspection sheet.

The next step was mine. When Lio asked me to check a measurement, I didn't take the pencil. I asked them to read the numbers aloud. We compared the marked board with the drawing and found one discrepancy together.

It took longer.

It was better.

After lunch we met with the person who had ordered the skiff. A market gardener named Sela needed a shallow boat for moving small tools during flood season. She wanted a low step, a stable handhold, and space for a crate that wouldn't slide when the deck got wet.

Lio had designed the boat with a lovely sweeping curve that would leave very little flat space.

They looked at the drawing, then at Sela.

"I could change the seat," they said.

"Would that weaken it?" she asked.

"Not if I adjust the support."

Maui opened his mouth.

He closed it again.

Lio looked at him.

"Would you check the lashing after I've made the change?"

"Gladly."

It was a tiny moment, and it felt like something important had shifted.

The work continued for another week. We didn't suddenly become perfect mentors. Once, Maui started lifting a whole rib into place before Lio had asked for help. Once, I corrected a label that had merely been written differently from the way I preferred.

Both times Fen raised an eyebrow.

Both times we stopped.

When the skiff was finally ready for the first water test, the whole cove gathered despite Lio's request for a small audience. The line of people along the shore looked like a festival crowd.

Lio stared at them.

"I don't want a speech," they muttered.

Maui was holding a rolled piece of paper.

He looked down at it.

Then at Lio.

"No speech," he agreed.

He put the paper away.

I loved him a little more for that.

The boat went into the water carefully. Fen checked the trim. Tamsin measured how low it sat with the first crates aboard. Sela stepped onto the deck and tested the handhold. It was not perfect. The second seat needed to move an inch, and the floor got slippery when a wave came over the bow.

Lio wrote both things down.

"Can I fix them before we call it finished?" they asked.

Fen smiled.

"That's the point."

We ate bread on the shore afterward. Maui had sand in his hair and a smear of chalk along his wrist. He looked tired in a way that made me think he'd actually been working instead of performing.

"How was teaching?" I asked.

"Harder than fighting monsters."

"Less applause."

"Far less."

He took my hand.

"How was not helping?"

"Terrible."

He laughed.

I leaned against his shoulder. The skiff rocked softly against its line, unfinished but real.

"When I first met you," I said, "I thought you were the person who knew what to do."

"And now?"

"Now I think the best thing you know is how to learn."

He kissed my forehead.

"Don't spread that around. It'll ruin my reputation."

I grinned.

Lio called from the slipway.

"Maui! I need help with the final knot!"

Maui stood, then paused.

"Do you want me to tie it?" he called.

"No. I want you to watch."

His smile changed.

"Coming."

I watched him go, carrying nothing but his patience.
